1:
The difference between the first tables and the second is what everyone notices. Henry states it simply: before, God provided the tables and wrote on them; now Moses hews them and God will only write. He turns the change into a history of revelation: when the law was first written on the heart of man in innocency both tables and writing were God's work, and only when that was broken did God take up the ministry of men to preserve his law in scripture — yet the prophets and apostles did no more than hew the tables, the writing being God's still. Wesley follows him closely. Ellicott puts the same thing as a maxim, that something is always lost by sin even when it is forgiven. Calvin is the sternest. Lest a readiness to pardon should breed indifference, God would leave some trace of the punishment behind, like a scar that remains after the wound has healed; the people are humbled by this one mark, that the stones which carried the covenant were not fashioned by God's hand nor quarried out of the sacred mount.

Who wrote on them is a harder question. Ellicott says it is quite clear, though some have held otherwise, that the second tables were inscribed by the finger of God, and with the same words. Keil and Delitzsch draw a smaller distinction from the Hebrew, since the first are called tables of stone and the second tables of stones; they take this for no sign of differing records but for the plain fact that Moses cut his from two separate blocks, while of God's nobody could say whether he had used one stone or two. Clarke faces the difficulty squarely, since a later verse of this chapter seems to make Moses the writer while Deuteronomy says expressly that God wrote the second tables as it wrote the first. His solution is that both are true of different documents: God engraved the commandments on the tables laid up in the ark, and Moses wrote a copy for the congregation, authenticated by being taken under God's direction, the original kept as the record against which later copies might be checked. He finds support in the phrase after the tenor of these words, literally according to the mouth of them, as though the original writing were giving out a copy of itself.

The last thing commanded is solitude. Ellicott marks how new the stringency was, since before this Aaron and the elders had climbed part of the way and Joshua had gone almost to the summit; now no one is to be seen anywhere on it, which he connects with the glory Moses had been promised he should see. Gill reads the exclusion as discipline: those who had sinned in the calf were shut out, and Joshua with them though he had no part in it, so that the giving of the law might be by Moses only. Calvin will not guess at the reason, saying the answer must remain with God, but he sees what the arrangement gained. Had the writing simply appeared on empty tables the miracle would have been more brilliant, yet God left room for faith by using a man's hand; and the proof was strong enough, since the people had watched Moses carry the tables up blank and there was no chisel on the mountain. Henry notices that God did not alter his measures although the last long absence had produced the calf: Moses shall stay as long as before, to try whether they had learned to wait. He notes too that Moses rose early, and adds that the morning is as good a friend to the graces as it is to the muses. On the hewing itself Henry and Gill both read it inward, the heart of stone having to be cut by conviction before God will write his law on it.
5:
The cloud that met him is the same one they had been following. Gill and Wesley identify it with the pillar that had gone before Israel and stood at the tent door the day before, now risen over the mountain. Ellicott follows its movement more closely: it withdrew from the door when Moses left off communing there and seemed to vanish, then became visible again at the summit and came down where he stood. Henry reads the descent as condescension, God humbling himself to notice a man who had humbled himself to walk with him, and thinks the cloud was meant to keep awe alive, lest the familiarity should breed contempt. Calvin adds what the sight did for the people below. They watched the cloud take Moses into it, so that after forty days out of the common life of men he might come forth like a new man, and the sight went to awaken their faith in the commandments he brought down. He warns against pressing the word descended, since God fills heaven and earth and does not shift his position; it answers to human perception, and Scripture gives the sacred name to the visible symbol, not because an empty cloud stood for an absent God but because it testified his presence.

What was proclaimed there Henry and Calvin both treat as the preface to the second giving of the law. Henry notes that it was done in passing, and draws a rule from it: fixed views of God are reserved for the future state, and the best we have here are transient. He sets two disclosures side by side — at the bush God made himself known in the glory of his self-existence, and here in the glory of his grace — and thinks a second edition of the law fitly prefaced by goodness, since it is goodness that gives a remedial law at all. The proclaiming of it, Henry adds, shows how far the mercy reaches, for he is good not to Israel only but to all. Calvin notices the doubling of the name for emphasis, and allows that the phrase about calling on the name may be read either of God proclaiming his own titles or of Moses professing his piety, finding no absurdity in either.

On the attributes themselves the two run close together. Henry insists that greatness and goodness set each other off: we are told how good God is lest the terror of his greatness make us afraid, and how great he is lest we presume on his goodness — these are not the mercies of a man, frail and fickle, but sure and sovereign mercies, which may be trusted but not tempted. He takes the words in order. Merciful bespeaks a father's compassion, and stands first because pity is the first wheel in all God's good-will to fallen man; gracious adds freeness, a complacency in creatures arising from his own will and not from anything in them; long-suffering means slow to anger, waiting to be gracious; and abundant in goodness and truth means goodness above our deserts, the springs of mercy always full and the streams always flowing. Calvin dwells on the same patience, as though God would abstain from severity if man's wickedness did not compel him, and on the pairing of mercy with truth, which he says the Psalms never separate, since mercy cannot be grasped except on the testimony of a word we can be sure of. He weighs the two numbers against each other, mercy to a thousand generations and punishment to the third and fourth, and concludes that clemency surpasses judgment; and he observes that the pardon covers not light offences only but the grossest, and a sinner who has offended a hundred times. Lest that be turned into a licence, the clause that will by no means clear the guilty is added by way of correction.
6:
Clarke treats the verse as God's own definition of his name. He would render it and proclaimed Jehovah, meaning that Moses was now shown what the august name contains, and he is impatient with the long history of guessing at it — some holding it inexplicable, some that it denotes the essence of the divine nature, some parcelling its letters out among the persons of the Trinity and the incarnation, which he says gives very little satisfaction. How strange, he asks, that none of these learned men noticed that God interprets the name here himself. He then counts eleven titles in the two verses and glosses each: Jehovah; the strong God; the merciful one, full of tenderness; the gracious one, whose nature is goodness itself; the long-suffering, not easily irritated; the mighty; the bountiful, exuberant in beneficence; the true one, who can neither deceive nor be deceived; the preserver of bountifulness, whose kindness runs on while the world endures; the bearer away of iniquity, whose prerogative alone it is to forgive; and last the God who visits iniquity, from whose justice no sinner escapes. Ellicott says much the same in fewer words, that this new name is not a name as we use the word but a description by accumulated epithets, and he arranges the three great disclosures in order: at the bush God showed his self-existence, in the descent on Sinai his terribleness, and now, in the act of pardoning, his mercy.

Wesley works over the same words with a different accent. He dwells on the abundance, that there is mercy enough in God, enough for all, enough for each, enough for ever, and reads goodness and truth together as goodness engaged by promise. Of the mercy kept for thousands he says it is never exhausted, since God gives to some and still keeps for others, and that its line is drawn parallel with eternity itself. Pardon he takes to be named last among the mercies because divine grace is most magnified in it, and because it opens the door to every other gift. Gill finds the same largeness written into the page, reporting that the first letter of the word for keeping is drawn longer than usual in the Hebrew text, which the Jews took for a sign of how far this grace extends. The clause that closes the proclamation is where the versions part company. Clarke sets them side by side: the Hebrew is literally in clearing he will not clear; the Samaritan changes one letter and gets with whom the innocent shall be innocent; the Arabic has he justifies and is not justified; one Greek copy makes it the guilty he will not cleanse with a purification-offering; and the Vulgate paraphrases it as no man being innocent of himself before God, which Clarke thinks a sound sense, since none can atone for his own sin. Wesley narrows the clause instead, to the impenitently guilty and to those who would be cleared without satisfaction to justice, and balances it by noting that God does not keep his anger for ever but visits to the third and fourth generation only, while he keeps mercy for thousands. Ellicott gives the reason the clause is there at all: to prevent the fatal misapprehension that God is a being of pure and mere benevolence.
8: Moses does not wait for the voice to finish. Gill has him hurry because he perceived it ceasing and the Lord passing on, and feared to lose the opportunity. Calvin reads the haste as astonishment, since God when he reveals himself so ravishes the godly with admiration that they have no leisure to deliberate what they should do but are struck down at once. Ellicott admires the combination in him, an ardent desire to look into the things of God joined with a reverence that would not look until the glory had gone by; Wesley finds in the same gesture his joy in the discovery, his thanks for it, and his submission to a justice he had just heard proclaimed along with the mercy. The prayer that follows turns the worst thing about Israel into the reason for the request. Wesley states the paradox plainly: God had given their stiff neck as his reason for not going with them, and Moses answers that the worse they are the more they need him, since he can neither bear with them nor rule them himself, but God will, being God and not man. Calvin reads the last petition as the argument of the whole, taking the phrase about possessing them causally, as though God could not enjoy the inheritance he had chosen except by pardoning their sins; and he applies it beyond that generation, since our own progress in grace is nothing but a continual reconciling. Ellicott lists what was asked — that God would go up in the midst of them, that he would forgive their iniquity when they offended in the way, and that he would attach them to himself permanently by making them his inheritance — and notes that no direct answer is given to any of it, the prayer being accepted indirectly by the renewal of the covenant, and Clarke observes that the title Moses uses here is not Jehovah but Adonai, which he takes to point to the Angel of the Covenant. Gill reads the opening words as certainty rather than doubt, since a man who had just seen the glory pass could hardly wonder whether he had found favour; he takes it for granted and builds on it. Wesley makes the same point about the whole prayer, which asks for nothing God had not already promised. Moses prays for these things not because he doubts the sincerity of the grant, but because he is anxious to have it ratified.
10:
Henry marks who is speaking. When the covenant was broken it was Israel that broke it; now that it is renewed it is God who makes it, so that if there are quarrels we bear all the blame and if there is peace God has all the glory. Wesley says the same. Calvin notes that the text does not say with whom the covenant is made, and reports that some supply the name of Moses; but since Moses stipulated for all, the sense comes to the same, that God makes it openly with the whole people. Ellicott spells out the terms: God will go with them, drive out the nations, work marvels, enlarge their borders and keep their enemies from coveting their land at the festivals, while they must observe what he commands this day — a command taking in both the ten words and a summary of the older book of the covenant, which is thereby republished.

The marvels promised are read forward into Joshua. Clarke, Ellicott and Wesley point to the same events: the drying up of Jordan, the fall of the walls of Jericho, the sun standing still, the hailstones on the five kings. Henry calls covenant blessings marvellous things and observes that these were without precedent, at once the joy of Israel and the terror of their enemies. Calvin puts the purpose differently, that God would deal so wonderfully with the nations as to prove himself the peculiar God of this people and distinguish them from the rest, exactly as Moses had prayed; and he notes that all were to be eye-witnesses of it, so that being convinced by their own senses they might submit sincerely to his dominion. Keil and Delitzsch describe the structure instead: to recall the duties of the covenant, the Lord repeats two leading points from the rights of Israel already given, the warning against any league with the Canaanites and the instructions for his own worship, and these are the main pillars meant to carry the renewed covenant.

The warning against alliances is read as a fence rather than a commandment. Henry treats the two great precepts as worshipping no other god and making no molten god, and the prohibitions before them as fences round both: they must not befriend idolaters lest they be tempted to their gods, and must destroy the altars and groves lest in time they use them or take pattern by them. He presses the reasonableness of it: if God makes war with the Canaanites, let Israel not make peace with them; if God takes care they shall not be Israel's lords, let Israel take care they be not its snares. On intermarriage he states the principle bluntly, that such is the corruption of nature that the bad are likelier to debauch the good than the good to reform the bad: those in league with idolaters come by degrees to love idolatry, and those who eat of the sacrifice will end by offering it. Wesley abridges the same argument. Gill points out that the caution is addressed not to Moses but to the people, against the day they should possess the land, and that the altars were to be thrown down lest they stand as temptations to sacrifice on them. Calvin reaches further than either. He grants that the command to destroy cannot be pressed on us as it stood, since God does not now bid us put the wicked to death, nor is any country assigned to the Church; yet he insists the case has reference to us, since those who voluntarily unite themselves with the ungodly put a yoke on their own necks. He then draws the distinction he thinks necessary: we cannot escape the ordinary dealings of life with unbelievers without going out of the world, but closer ties — alliances between nations, marriages between persons — open the door to Satan.
14:
Ellicott defends the divine jealousy against those who find it unworthy of God. That the one only God, if there is but one, should claim an undivided allegiance and exact it under severe penalties is natural and reasonable, and agrees with the most exalted view of his nature; indifference to idolatry would mean that he cared little for his creatures, like the god of Epicurus, who having once made the world paid it no further attention. The same writer explains why the altars and groves had to go: retained, they could only lead on to the worship of the gods they were dedicated to, since they could be kept for no other purpose, so their destruction follows as a corollary from the second commandment. On molten gods he offers a suggestion about the calf, that the makers of it may have supposed themselves clear of a commandment which forbade only graven images, so that an express law against molten ones was now needed. Gill reads the word as a part standing for the whole, graven images being included, but thinks molten ones named because they were chiefly what the Canaanites worshipped, and above all because the calf had been one.

Calvin takes the same prohibition down to its root. When statues and pictures are called gods, he says, the sum of the second commandment appears: God is insulted when he is clothed in a corporeal image. He is careful about what the heathen actually believed. They did not suppose the deity shut up in corruptible material, but imagined it nearer to them if some earthly symbol stood before their eyes, thinking they could not climb to the height where God dwells unless they mounted by such aids. On the choice of metal he is equally careful: gold is no more abominable to God than wood or stone, but since the insane zeal of superstition is the more inflamed by a costly material or a fine piece of workmanship, molten gods are condemned by name. He adds that the word used for idols carries its own contempt, being applied to statues and stones and graven images alike to mark them with ignominy.

Then the feasts return, and Henry sees why they are repeated here. When the people made the calf they proclaimed a feast in its honour; now, that they may never do so again, they are charged with keeping the feasts God himself appointed. He draws the general lesson that no one needs to be drawn away from religion by the promise of mirth, since we serve a Master who has provided abundantly for the joy of his servants, serious godliness being a continual feast. On the weekly rest he presses the hardest case, that it holds in earing time and in harvest, when business is busiest: all worldly work must give way to it, and harvest will prosper the better for the sabbath being kept in harvest time. Keil and Delitzsch set out the whole calendar in order, the unleavened bread and the firstlings, the rest on the seventh day, the feast of weeks at the wheat harvest and the ingathering at the year's end, with the three yearly appearances. Henry answers the objection that suggests itself, that a country emptied of its men three times a year lay open to its neighbours. The promise meets it exactly, since they shall not so much as desire the land; all hearts are in God's hands, and he can restrain not only men's actions but their wishes. From that he takes his rule, that the way of duty is the way of safety, and that those employed in God's work are under a special protection while they are about it.
21:
Ellicott observes how often this one law comes round in the book. It is so fundamental to the whole polity that it appears in every section of the legislation — at the giving of the manna, in the fourth commandment, in the book of the covenant, and appended to the directions for the tabernacle. He glosses the old English of our version, earing time being ploughing time, from a verb related to the Greek and Latin words for tilling, and notes that the two seasons named are precisely those at which there was a special temptation to encroach on the rest. Clarke takes that temptation as the point of the verse and presses it hard. Many break the sabbath on a plea of necessity, reckoning that if the weather has been bad through harvest and the sabbath comes fine, the fineness of the day is itself a providential indication that it should be used; and he asks whether this command is not aimed directly at that reasoning. He adds what he has observed, that he has known the law often broken on that pretence and has never found such men prosper one whit better than their more conscientious neighbours. Gill notes only that the law is repeated to fix it in their minds, and Wesley that we show by keeping it which we prefer, our communion with God or the business and the joy of harvest.

The three yearly appearances raise an obvious difficulty, and the promise attached to them answers it. Clarke states the difficulty as a soldier might: with the men gone up, nothing was left to hold the fenced cities but women and children, and the surrounding nations could have taken the whole country at their leisure. That they never did he treats as a standing proof of the divine origin of the religion, and as a barrier no deistical mind can get over — three times a year God worked a special miracle for his people, controlling not their enemies' actions only but their wishes. Wesley makes the same point in a line, that they were not merely kept from invading but from so much as thinking of it, and calls it a standing miracle through so many generations. Ellicott finds a partial parallel among the Greeks, whose unwritten law gave free passage to anyone travelling to or from the great national festivals, but says the promise here goes far beyond any such understanding, since it secures the whole territory from attack at those seasons. On the enlarging of the borders he traces a double promise and a double fulfilment: Canaan alone was pledged to Abraham at first and afterwards the whole tract from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates, and Israel first held Canaan only, then under Solomon reached the Euphrates, then shrank again at the rebellion of Jeroboam.

Three older laws are appended at the close, and the commentators treat them as citations rather than novelties. Gill takes the first to mean that the passover was not to be killed while any leaven remained in the houses, and Clarke identifies the sacrifice named as the paschal lamb. On the firstfruits and on the kid seethed in its mother's milk, Gill, Clarke and Ellicott alike do no more than point back to the same three rules as they stood in the book of the covenant, which is the plainest sign of what this whole passage is: not a new code but the old one re-issued to a people who had broken it.
28:
Ellicott admits the length is surprising at first sight, since by now there were no fresh instructions to give; the answer he takes from Deuteronomy, that the time was spent in a long and earnest intercession which at last prevailed and turned away the anger. Gill is interested in the count, and reckons this a third period of forty days rather than a repetition of the first, noting that Jewish writers and several learned Christians alike make three such stays on the mountain, and that the dates come out exactly. Calvin explains why the number had to be the same. Had Moses been kept there only a few days, his authority would not have been ratified by any conspicuous miracle; the forty days obtained full credit for his mission, and were needed so that the second tables should stand no lower than the first.

On the fast itself Calvin is careful to say what kind of thing it was. This was no fast of temperance or sobriety but of special privilege, an exemption from the infirmity of the flesh granted for a season so that the lawgiver's condition might differ from other men's: he felt no hunger, did not struggle with any longing for food, and wanted meat and drink no more than an angel does. That, Calvin says, is why the prophets never alleged it as an example and nobody attempted to imitate what everyone knew was not granted to them — Elijah excepted, who was sent to revive a law almost lost, like a second Moses, and Christ, who fasted so that his gospel might have no less credit than the law. From this he turns on the annual fast of the Church, which he thinks a gross error, since men without exception set themselves to rival the Son of God as though a new promulgation of the gospel had been entrusted to them, when Christ fasted forty days only once in his life and felt no hunger while he did. Ellicott makes the same restriction historically: fasts of this duration are recorded only of Moses, Elijah and our Lord, they are absolutely miraculous, and modern attempts to rival them are regarded by scientific men as owing whatever success they seem to have had to imposture.

Henry reads the forty days as communion rather than endurance. Moses was with God without interruption and did not think it long, and Henry turns that on the reader: those who find an hour's attendance on God wearisome should think how many days and nights Moses spent there. He gives two reasons why the man needed nothing. The power of God supported him, since he who made the body can nourish it without the ordinary means; and his communion with God entertained him, so that he did not want food — he had meat to eat which the world knew not of, it being his meat and drink to hear God's word and pray. When God would entertain his favourite, Henry says, it was not with meat and drink but with his light and law and love. The verse ends by saying that he wrote the words of the covenant, and both Keil and Ellicott insist the subject is God and not Moses. Ellicott grants that the clause standing by itself would naturally suggest the other reading, but holds that the Hebrew idiom allows Jehovah as the nominative and that it must be so taken to agree with the opening of the chapter and with Deuteronomy; the second tables were written with the finger of God as truly as the first. Henry sets one comparison against all this that keeps the honour in proportion: our Lord's face shone as the sun and his clothing with it, yet coming down from his mountain he laid that glory aside, it being his will that we should walk by faith and not by sight.
29:
The word for the shining is a strange one, and Clarke makes the most of it. It means to send out horns, and so is used of rays darting from a polished surface, which is why he supposes the glory filling the man's soul broke out in points of light. He blames the Latin version for rendering it that his face was horned, and asks, if the word is to be pressed, why the painters gave him only two, when there must have been hundreds of such rays. He then traces the halo of art to this verse, since almost every nation that has heard the story has drawn men of extraordinary sanctity with a circle of light about the head, Greek and Roman saints and the holy men of the Mohammedans and Hindoos alike. Ellicott insists the phenomenon was physical and not figurative, citing the apostle's comment on it, and reports the view that such radiance once belonged to man as part of the image of God, was forfeited at the fall, and is restored now and then to particular saints — to Moses here, to Elijah on the mount, to Stephen before the council — while it belonged in surpassing measure to the human nature of Christ, concealed for the most part but shown at the transfiguration. He too rejects the horns as a mistranslation, and would render the phrase not while he talked with him but through his talking with him.

Why Moses did not know is a question in itself. Keil and Delitzsch state the fact simply, that the sight of the glory, though only of its back or reflection, so wrought on the skin of his face that it shone without his observing it. Calvin thinks it was hidden from him for a time on purpose, so that he might come down freely and the miracle be the more evident when seen close at hand. Wesley takes the shining as an honour done to the man, so that the people might never again question his mission or speak slightly of him: he carried his credentials in his very countenance. Wesley passes on the opinion that some remainder of the glory stayed with him as long as he lived, since that eye could not grow dim which had seen God, nor that face wrinkle which had shone with his glory.

The people's fear is read as conscience rather than dazzlement. Clarke says the sight alarmed them because their consciences were still guilty from the late transgression and they had not yet received the atonement, and adds that the appearance of superior sanctity often awes the guilty into respect. Wesley thinks it not only dazzled their eyes but struck such an awe on them that they had to retire, and that they could not tell whether the light was a token of favour or of displeasure. Gill limits who saw it, taking those who met him at the foot of the mountain to be the princes rather than the whole people, who could not have seen him all at once. Calvin turns the fear into a rebuke. The question why Moses could bear the glory of God while the people could not bear the rays reflected from a man's face he answers by saying they were branded with that mark of disgrace to make them confess how far their ingratitude had carried them from God, since Moses came down from speaking with God securely and they shrank from the sight of a mortal.
31:
When the veil went on is disputed, and the difference is not small. Gill takes our version as it stands and will not have the Greek reading, that Moses veiled himself when he had finished; on that reading, he says, there would have been no occasion for the veil at all. His account is that Moses covered his face as soon as he perceived the glory the people could not bear, and went on speaking to Aaron and the rulers and then to the congregation with the veil already on. Ellicott says flatly that the English exactly inverts the sense, which is that the veil went on when the speaking was over. On his reading the veil became part of the man's ordinary dress, laid aside on two occasions only: when he went in alone to God, where he spoke face to face without it, and when he came out with a message, which he authenticated by uncovering and letting the brightness be seen. Clarke follows the same rule in reverse order, having Moses veiled whenever he addressed the people in public and unveiled whenever he entered the tabernacle. Gill notes at the close that nobody can say how long the shining lasted, though one rabbi held it never left him to the day of his death, and Aben Ezra and many learned men after him thought it continued as long as he lived.

What the veil meant is where the commentators spend their strength. Wesley reads it as the darkness of that whole dispensation: the ceremonial institutions had much of Christ and the gospel in them, but a covering was drawn over it, so that Israel could not see distinctly the good things to come of which the law held the shadow. He puts it in three figures — beauty veiled, gold still in the mine, a pearl in the shell — and adds that by the gospel the veil is taken off the old testament, though it lies still on the hearts of those who shut their eyes against the light. On the unveiling before God he draws the practical rule, that every veil must be thrown aside when we present ourselves to the Lord, and hears in it the promise that when a soul turns to the Lord the covering is removed, so that with open face it may behold the glory.

Clarke builds the same contrast on a larger scale. As the glory of Moses' face was real and yet was swallowed up in the splendour of God when he went into the tabernacle, so the brightness of the Mosaic dispensation is eclipsed by the gospel: one was the shadow and the other is the substance. He sets the two side by side without softening either. The law showed sin in its exceeding sinfulness, and the justice and purity of God with it, but of itself made no provision for pardon; the gospel exhibits the Lamb of God putting away sin by the sacrifice of himself. The one was a ministration of death which ministered terror, so that the high priest feared to approach and the mediator himself trembled; by the other men have boldness to enter the holiest. He then reads the veil twice over as a figure — of the ceremonies themselves, each covering a spiritual meaning the Jews never lifted it to find, and of the darkness that came on them when they refused the gospel — and finds a survival of it still, since a Jew reading the law in the synagogue draws a tasselled woollen cloth over his head, which Clarke takes for a standing emblem of the covering the apostle says lies on the heart whenever Moses is read.
